title: The one who escaped
hook: Abd al-Rahman, an Umayyad prince, escapes to Spain and founds a new state

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fall, black banners and the end of Umayyad rule. Your line was dynasties fall.

A young man is sitting in a house near the Euphrates when his small son runs in, frightened. Outside, black banners: the Abbasid horsemen have come for what is left of the Umayyad family. He grabs his younger brother and they run for the river. They plunge in and swim. From the bank, the soldiers shout: come back, you're safe, nobody will harm you. The younger brother, tired and afraid of drowning, turns back. The older one keeps swimming. From the far bank, the histories say, he watched them kill his brother. His name was Abd al-Rahman, a grandson of the caliph Hisham. Today: the one who escaped.
screen: `BLACK BANNERS OUTSIDE.` → `INTO THE EUPHRATES.` → `ONE TURNS BACK, ONE SWIMS ON.`

segments.voice: What do you do when everything you belonged to is gone? Abd al-Rahman went west. The Andalusian histories say he traveled in hiding through North Africa with a freedman named Badr, staying for a time with his mother's people, the Berbers, and slipping away when local rulers grew suspicious. Al-Andalus, across the strait, was full of quarreling factions, and among them were old clients and supporters of the Umayyad house. Badr crossed first to sound them out. Then Abd al-Rahman landed. He gathered supporters, defeated the governor, and entered Cordoba as its ruler. He didn't claim to be caliph. He ruled as emir, and the state he founded would last long after him. People gave him a nickname, al-Dakhil, the one who entered. And there's a tender story people tell. In a garden near Cordoba, he is said to have planted a palm tree, the kind that grew back in Syria, and written lines of poetry to it. In the poem, as the story goes, he speaks to the palm as a fellow stranger: you too are far from your home, brought to a land not your own. So the founder of a state is remembered talking to a tree about homesickness. He lost much of his family, his city and his world, and he did not get them back. He started again, in a new place, with what he carried.
screen: `WEST THROUGH NORTH AFRICA.` · `BADR CROSSES FIRST.` · `CORDOBA, AND AN EMIR.` · then, large: `A PALM FAR FROM HOME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time something ended for you, a move, a loss, a door that closed, and notice what you carried out of it, even something small: a habit, a friend, a skill, a stubbornness. If you pray, ask for strength for new beginnings in your own words; if you don't, just let what you carried be counted.
Al-Dakhil, the one who enters: the nickname given to Abd al-Rahman, the Umayyad prince who swam the Euphrates and founded a new state in al-Andalus. Today's word.
Your line: he started again. Homesick and far from home, and still beginning. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: The story of Abd al-Rahman's escape and his palm-tree poem is retold in histories of al-Andalus, and the Great Mosque of Cordoba, which tradition says he began, still stands.
